Project: YCompany eClaims | Version 1.0 | Author: Utsav Verma (Senior Staff Engineer, Nagarro) | Date: 07-Jul-2026 | Classification: Confidential

Web · Staff · Partner Portals

Layer 2 — API Gateway / Ingress
WAF · CDN · ALB · Auth

Layer 4 — Async / Messaging
EventBridge · SQS · SNS · Lambda

Notes & Conventions:
1. All external traffic is HTTPS / TLS 1.2+. Inter-service calls carry an OAuth2 JWT (15-min access / 7-day refresh), validated against the Auth Service.
2. Layer 6 platform services (IAM/SSO, KMS, CloudWatch, X-Ray, CloudTrail, CI/CD, Terraform) are cross-cutting and govern every layer above — shown by a representative dashed flow (KMS → data at rest).
3. All data is encrypted at rest (KMS AES-256) and in transit (TLS 1.2+); every claim document and customer communication is archived in S3 for audit and compliance.
4. Solid arrows = request / data flow (protocol labelled). Dashed arrows = cross-cutting / governance / association.

Why no managed API Gateway? Classic API-Gateway capabilities are already delivered by existing components (verified against the SAD):
Routing / dispatch → ALB (Multi-AZ, /claims /auth)   |   AuthN / AuthZ → Auth Service (OAuth2/JWT) + RBAC + Okta SSO, ALB OIDC offload
Rate limiting / throttling → AWS WAF + Shield (edge rate-based rules)   |   Caching → CloudFront (edge) + ElastiCache Redis (data, <100 ms)
Canary / blue-green → CodePipeline + CodeDeploy, ALB weighted target groups   |   Circuit breaker / retries → service-level breakers + exponential backoff
Distributed tracing → CloudWatch + X-Ray   |   Request validation → in-service (FastAPI + Pydantic)
A managed API Gateway would only add per-API-key usage plans / metering — not required, since partners integrate via the Partner Portal, not raw metered APIs.

1. Route 53 (G1) is the network entry point — DNS resolution and health-checked routing — added per review feedback; not originally named in the SAD's prose but operationally necessary for any internet-facing deployment (now also named in SAD §4 Layer 2).
2. Every AWS component on this page and the CI/CD page uses real AWS Architecture Icons and proper AWS group containers (VPC/AZ/Subnet/Security-Group) — a departure from pages 1-4's plain colour-block convention, scoped to these two infrastructure pages only.
3. Phase 1 = single AWS Region, Multi-AZ (3 zones) only; multi-region active-active DR is Phase 2 (§9). The specific region is not stated in the case study and is shown pending confirmation.
4. This page is the deployment-topology companion to page 4 — page 4 names every AWS service per logical layer; this page places the same services on a physical VPC/AZ/subnet network map.
5. V1–V6 are tagged once, in Zone A, to avoid clutter; Zones B/C repeat the pattern untagged. Zone C's data subnet is deliberately sparser — RDS/ElastiCache Multi-AZ is a standard 2-AZ pair; only the 3-node OpenSearch domain needs a third zone for write quorum.
6. The Data Subnet reuses the Private Subnet's group-container styling — AWS's icon set has no distinct "isolated subnet" container; isolation is conveyed by the label, not a different icon.
7. Perpendicular line crossings are expected and handled by this file's jumpStyle=arc convention — not a duplicate/overlapping path. What's eliminated is any two edges sharing a coincident parallel route.
8. The Auth Service is grouped under Layer 2 in SAD §4 for its logical capability, but physically runs as an ECS Fargate task in the private/app subnet alongside every other microservice.
9. Every component sits behind a Security Group; one is drawn illustratively around the Zone-A Fargate icon rather than repeated on every instance.
10. AWS SNS and SES appear twice by design: N4 is the internal EventBridge-driven pub/sub; D4/D5 represent the last-mile hop out to the carrier/mail server — two different network hops through the same managed service, not a duplicate.
11. CI/CD (CodePipeline/CodeBuild/CodeDeploy/ECR, SAD §4 Layer 6/§8) has its own dedicated page (tab 6) rather than being drawn here — it's a deployment-time concern, not a runtime network path.

Notes & Conventions:
1. Reading order: Source (P1) → CodePipeline (P2) orchestrates three sequential stages via a shared S3 artifact bucket (P3) — Stage 1 Build (P4→P5), Stage 2 Infrastructure (P6, Terraform, manual approval gate), Stage 3 Deploy (P7, blue/green).
2. Cost framing: CodePipeline charges a small flat fee per active pipeline with no idle-time charge; CodeBuild bills only actual build-minutes — no idle build server to provision, patch or scale. Materially cheaper than a self-managed Jenkins controller running around the clock, and avoids a second CI/CD tool alongside AWS's own managed equivalents.
3. Blue/Green mechanism: Blue = current/live (P10), Green = new candidate (P11); CodeDeploy (P7) shifts ALB weighted-target-group traffic (P8) — the mechanism behind SAD §7's "blue-green deployment for zero-downtime releases."
4. Rollback: A CloudWatch (R1) alarm on ECS/ALB health during the traffic shift triggers automated traffic-back-to-Blue and Green deregistration — ties to §7's Resilience/Reliability row.
5. CodeBuild appears twice (P4, P6) — two distinct projects (app build/test, Terraform plan/apply), one managed service; mirrors the Cloud/Deployment page's own SNS/SES dual-appearance note.
6. CloudWatch (R1) and Secrets Manager/KMS/IAM (Q1-Q3) also appear on the Cloud/Deployment page (N7-N10) — same services, two different lifecycle moments (steady-state runtime there, deployment-time here), not a duplicate.
7. This page is a companion to the Cloud/Deployment page — it does not redraw the VPC/AZ/subnet topology. The ECS Service/task-set icons here stand in for the same Multi-AZ Fargate runtime (V3 there); the ALB (P8) is the same Multi-AZ ALB (V1 there), not a second load balancer.
8. Q3 (IAM) is shown with no drawn edge, consistent with the Cloud/Deployment page's N9 — its role relationship applies uniformly to every pipeline stage.
9. Source Repository (P1) is rendered in the same to-be-confirmed/assumption style as the Policy Administration System (E3) on pages 1 and 5 — no source-control platform is named anywhere in the case study or SAD.
Each domain owns its data and services; domains integrate only through published events on the messaging backbone (loose coupling).
